title: Across the Chessboard
cardDescription: Meet familiar chess pieces and board words through direct clues about their shapes, positions, and roles.
description: Meet familiar chess pieces and board words through direct clues about their shapes, positions, and roles.
focus: The clues identify chess vocabulary without presenting a position to solve. Some answers name a piece; others name a board feature, a result, or an action.
solvingTip: Check whether the clue asks for a piece, a board feature, or a playing term. Short color and turn words can help cross the longer piece names.

answerNotes.RANK: A rank is a horizontal row on the board. A file is a vertical column, so orientation distinguishes the terms.
answerNotes.FILE: File is a chess column here. It does not mean a document or a workshop smoothing tool.
answerNotes.KNIGHT: The knight is conventionally shown with a horse head. Its L-shaped movement helps distinguish it from other pieces.
answerNotes.ROOK: Rook is the formal piece name. Castle describes its familiar tower shape and also appears as a separate move term.
answerNotes.MATE: Mate is short for checkmate. Being in check alone is different because a legal response may still be available.
answerNotes.DRAW: A draw is a result with no winner. The clue does not use draw for taking a card or making a picture.

cardDescription: Explore American checkers through familiar board colors, jumping pieces, and words for crowning and capturing.
description: Explore American checkers through familiar board colors, jumping pieces, and words for crowning and capturing.
focus: The clues use American checkers terminology. Direct definitions describe pieces and board features rather than asking for a move from a diagram.
solvingTip: Look for a game name, a piece, a board feature, or an action. An ordinary piece and a crowned piece have different terms. Short color words can help with longer game vocabulary.

answerNotes.DRAUGHTS: Draughts is the British game name. American English commonly calls the game checkers.
answerNotes.MAN: Man is a traditional term for an uncrowned checker. In this clue it names a piece rather than a person.
answerNotes.KING: A king is a promoted piece. In American checkers, it can move diagonally in both forward and backward directions.
answerNotes.CROWN: Crown is a verb for promotion here. A second disk is often stacked on the piece to show its new status.
answerNotes.DIAGONAL: Diagonal means slanting across the board's grid. It differs from a horizontal row or vertical column.
answerNotes.JUMP: A jump passes over another piece. The clue identifies the movement rather than a named player or a final score.

title: Dominoes on the Table
cardDescription: Set out familiar domino words for dotted tiles, matching ends, and simple actions around a game table.
description: Set out familiar domino words for dotted tiles, matching ends, and simple actions around a game table.
focus: The clues describe domino equipment and common playing vocabulary. Different domino games use different scoring rules, so the definitions stay with the objects and ordinary actions.
solvingTip: Ask whether the clue names a tile, a marking, an arrangement, or an action. Equal values on both ends identify a particular kind of tile. Short scoring and playing words can help with longer answers.

answerNotes.PIP: A pip is one dot. Its count contributes to a tile's value, so the clue asks for a marking rather than the whole tile.
answerNotes.DOUBLE: A double has equal values on both ends. It does not mean any random pair of two tiles.
answerNotes.BLANK: Blank means a zero-dot end here. It is a marked value category rather than a missing or damaged tile.
answerNotes.HAND: Hand is a player's held group of tiles. The clue does not mean the body part that physically holds them.
answerNotes.DRAW: Draw means take a tile in this clue. It is an action rather than a tied result.
answerNotes.SHUFFLE: Shuffling mixes the pieces before play. The word is used for tiles here, as it can also be for cards.

title: Inside a Deck of Cards
cardDescription: Open a deck through a familiar suit symbol, named cards, and the everyday words used to handle a hand.
description: Open a deck through a familiar suit symbol, named cards, and the everyday words used to handle a hand.
focus: This puzzle identifies card symbols and common playing actions. The clues describe the vocabulary without requiring the rules of a particular card game.
solvingTip: Check whether a clue asks for a suit symbol, a named card, a group, or an action. One playing card and the group held by a player have different names.

answerNotes.SUIT: A suit groups cards by symbol. It does not name clothing in this deck-related clue.
answerNotes.SPADE: Spade names a black card symbol here. The same word names a garden digging tool elsewhere.
answerNotes.CLUB: Club is a black suit symbol with three rounded lobes. Its shape distinguishes it from the pointed spade.
answerNotes.JOKER: A joker is an extra card used in some games. It is separate from the ordinary numbered and face cards of the four suits.
answerNotes.DEAL: Deal means distribute cards in this clue. It describes the action rather than a bargain or agreement.
answerNotes.TRICK: A trick is a group of played cards in certain games. The term does not mean deception in this playing context.

title: A Friendly Board-Game Evening
cardDescription: Gather around the table with familiar words for players, pieces, rules, and the results of a board game.
description: Gather around the table with familiar words for players, pieces, rules, and the results of a board game.
focus: The clues cover words shared by many games. Some answers name equipment, while others name a stage, a result, or the role of a participant. Individual games can use these terms in different ways.
solvingTip: Look for whether the clue names a player, a playing object, a stage, or a result. A cycle of play and equal final scores have different terms. Short result words can help cross longer playing objects.

answerNotes.DICE: Dice is the usual plural of die. The clue asking for more than one cube uses the plural form.
answerNotes.DIE: Die is singular in traditional game usage. The surrounding game context separates it from the unrelated verb about death.
answerNotes.TOKEN: A token stands for a player or position. It names the representative object rather than the person moving it.
answerNotes.ROUND: Round is a stage or cycle of play here. It is not a description of a circular shape.
answerNotes.TIE: A tie means equal scores in this clue. It does not name a garment or a fastening action.
answerNotes.TIMER: A timer measures a permitted interval. It differs from a scoreboard that records points rather than elapsed time.
